topics.topic: How duplicate ports in fields entries must be handled during canonicalization
questions: When two fields entries have the same port, must the object contain one member per entry and therefore repeat a member name, or must duplicate ports be rejected or otherwise reconciled before canonical_bytes is called?

quotes: content_identity: [BEHAVIOR] For the idempotency_key variant MUST build one JSON object with one member per entry of fields, named by the entry's port and holding the JSON value its canonical_json encodes, so the order of the fields does not change the key, and return the hexadecimal SHA-256 of its canonical bytes; a field whose value is null is kept as null, not dropped.

canonical_bytes: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST raise NonCanonicalValueError, with a reason naming the first offending item in text order, when json_text is not one well-formed JSON value, when an object repeats a member name at any depth, when it holds a non-finite number (NaN, Infinity or -Infinity tokens, which the default Python parser would accept and therefore MUST be rejected explicitly), when a number written without a fraction or exponent lies outside plus or minus (2 to the power 53 minus 1), which an IEEE double cannot hold exactly, or when a string holds a lone surrogate.
KeyFieldsContent fields (exact, no others exist): subject_kind: Literal['idempotency_key'], fields: tuple[JsonPayload, ...]
JsonPayload fields (exact, no others exist): payload_kind: Literal['json'], port: str, canonical_json: bytes
judgement.divergence: One implementer rejects repeated ports before hashing, while another reconciles them by retaining one value, such as the last entry; the caller notices an error instead of a digest, and different reconciliation rules can produce different digests.
judgement.why: The texts require a member for every entry but neither prohibit duplicate ports nor define how multiple entries with the same object-member name are reconciled.

topics.topic: Whether exceptions may be modified or wrapped so their reason identifies the failing startup step
questions: When an exception's original reason does not name the failing step, must it be propagated unchanged or modified/wrapped so that its reason names the step?

Must an exception propagate unchanged, or may it be altered or wrapped to add the failing step to its reason when that reason does not already name the step?

quotes: Every step is required: the first step that raises — InstallationRejectedError, RefusedError from the instance check, a store refusal, SandboxUnavailableError, StopRequiredError or any other exception — stops the sequence there and propagates unchanged to the caller with the step named in its reason; no later step runs and nothing is retried or skipped.

When run_start_sequence raises, MUST write the failing step and the exception's reason to standard error, without any token, credential value, configuration content or stack trace, open no entrance and return a non-zero exit code;
judgement.divergence: One implementation propagates the original exception unchanged even when its reason omits the step; another modifies or wraps it to add the step, and serve_kernel and its operator observe different exception identity and diagnostic text.
judgement.why: The requirement simultaneously demands unchanged propagation and a reason naming the step, which cannot both hold for an original reason that omits it.

judgement.why: The body is not read before size and token checks, so refusals at those checks cannot recover its id and use null.

topics.topic: Whether initialize, ping, and tools/list bypass catalogue-operation naming and authorization requirements
questions: Must every JSON-RPC request name and authorize a catalogue operation, or do initialize, ping and tools/list bypass those catalogue-operation checks?
Must every JSON-RPC request name a catalogue operation and call its handler, or are initialize, ping and tools/list exempt from those requirements?

quotes: MUST check one request in exactly this order, the first failure deciding: the byte length of request_bytes is within the imported RELEASE_CEILING_SURFACE_REQUEST_BYTES_MAX constant, else invalid_request; authenticate_token with presented_token gives an Actor, else unauthorized with one fixed reason that reveals nothing about any record; the message names a catalogue operation and fits that operation's request model with no unknown field — a field typed X | None fitting when it is absent or JSON null — and every bound below, else invalid_request; the actor may call that operation by the actor table, else not_permitted; only then is the operation's handler called (A16 rule 1).

A request's method decides: initialize answers the result {protocolVersion: the imported MCP_PROTOCOL_VERSION constant, capabilities: {tools: {listChanged: false}}, serverInfo: {name: the imported MCP_SERVER_NAME constant, version: the imported MCP_SERVER_VERSION constant}} whatever version its params ask, and keeps no state; ping answers an empty result object; tools/list answers {tools: [...]} as below, ignoring any cursor; tools/call names the catalogue operation in params.name and carries its request in params.arguments, which then pass the remaining checks of the first note.
judgement.divergence: One implementation rejects initialize, ping, and tools/list because they do not name catalogue operations; another handles them directly and applies catalogue fitting, authorization, and handler dispatch only to tools/call, which MCP callers observe.
judgement.why: The universal ordered-check requirement says every request must name and authorize a catalogue operation, while the method-specific passage assigns non-catalogue behavior to three request methods.

quotes: MUST check one request in exactly this order, the first failure deciding: the byte length of request_bytes is within the imported RELEASE_CEILING_SURFACE_REQUEST_BYTES_MAX constant, else invalid_request; authenticate_token with presented_token gives an Actor, else unauthorized with one fixed reason that reveals nothing about any record;
The body is one JSON-RPC 2.0 message, read only after the size and token checks.

A JSON object whose jsonrpc is "2.0" with a string method and an id is a request; one with a method and no id is a notification and one with no method a response: both are answered with empty bytes and change nothing.
judgement.why: Size and token checks occur before the body is read and classified, so an oversized or unauthenticated notification or response is refused before the empty-response rule can apply.

topics.topic: Whether supplied JSON texts are parsed for canonicalization inside the kernel process
questions: Must supplied JSON texts be interpreted as JSON to canonicalize them, or must they never be interpreted in the kernel process?

quotes: Before any handler runs, MUST replace every JSON text the request carries — the json_text of each RequestJsonValue and RequestConstant, the value_schema of every Port and RequestConstant, the guard_value of every EdgeGuard — by its canonical form obtained from canonical_bytes; a NonCanonicalValueError there is invalid_request, so modules below receive only canonical JSON (A01 rule 1).
Text an agent supplies — purposes, implementation code, names, JSON texts — is data: it is never evaluated, imported, compiled, formatted or interpreted in the kernel process;
judgement.divergence: One implementation parses and interprets supplied JSON texts through canonical_bytes to validate and canonicalize them; another treats the prohibition on interpretation literally and cannot perform that canonicalization, which callers observe through acceptance, rejection, and normalized values.
judgement.why: Obtaining canonical JSON necessarily interprets its JSON structure, while another passage expressly says supplied JSON texts are never interpreted in the kernel process.
